summary: Defines a MIB module for scheduling management operations, allowing network management actions to be set to run at specific times. It was replaced by RFC 3231.

eli5.summary: This is an alarm clock for network devices, so chores can be set to happen at chosen times.

questions: how to schedule network management tasks
subtitle: A way to schedule network management tasks to run at specific times and intervals.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to perform management tasks on a schedule—such as checking status at regular intervals, enabling or disabling interfaces during certain hours, or collecting statistics at specific times—but SNMP has no built-in way to schedule operations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2591 defines a MIB module with objects that describe three kinds of schedules: periodic (every N seconds), calendar-based (specific days, hours, and minutes), and one-shot (run once and disable). Each schedule specifies a MIB variable to modify and a value to write to it at the scheduled time.
tldr.outcome: Network devices that implement this scheduling MIB can automatically perform management operations without requiring a manager to repeatedly send commands, reducing the need for continuous network traffic and manual intervention.

today: RFC 2591 was obsoleted by RFC 3231, which provides an update to the scheduling MIB. The underlying concept of scheduling SNMP operations remains useful for network management automation.

sections.title: What Is Scheduling for Network Management
sections.content:
Network administrators often need to perform the same task repeatedly or at specific times. Examples include checking the status of a network interface at regular intervals, turning equipment on or off at certain hours, or collecting performance statistics. Rather than having a management system send the same command repeatedly, it is more efficient for the network device itself to perform these actions automatically on a schedule.

This RFC defines a standard way to configure such schedules using SNMP's Management Information Base (MIB). The schedules are defined as managed objects that can be read and modified through SNMP, allowing administrators to create, enable, disable, and monitor scheduled tasks on network devices.
sections.eli5: Instead of constantly asking a device to do something, you can tell it once to do it automatically on a schedule, like an alarm clock for network chores.

sections.title: Three Types of Schedules
sections.content:
The RFC defines three schedule types. Periodic schedules repeat at fixed time intervals. You specify the number of seconds between invocations (for example, every 600 seconds for a 10-minute interval). The scheduler ensures no action runs before the next scheduled interval, though local system load may cause delays.

Calendar schedules trigger based on calendar time: specific weekdays (Monday, Friday, etc.), months (January, June, etc.), days of the month (1st, 15th, etc.), hours (0-23), and minutes (0-59). You can combine multiple values—for example, run on every Monday and Friday at 9:00 AM and 3:00 PM in June and December.

One-shot schedules work like calendar schedules but automatically disable themselves after triggering once. These are useful for one-time administrative tasks.
sections.eli5: Periodic schedules are like "every 10 minutes". Calendar schedules are like "every Monday at 3 PM". One-shot schedules are like "next Friday at 2 PM, then stop".

sections.title: How Scheduling Actions Work
sections.content:
A scheduled action is defined by pointing to a MIB variable (an object identifier) and specifying a value to write to that variable when the schedule triggers. The MIB variable must be an INTEGER type. When the scheduled time arrives, the scheduler performs an SNMP set operation to write the specified value.

For example, an administrator might create a schedule that sets ifAdminStatus (interface administrative status) to down (0) at 8 PM on weekdays, effectively disabling the interface during off-hours. The scheduler enforces access control rules when performing these set operations, respecting the SNMP security framework.

Each schedule entry tracks operational status (enabled, disabled, or finished), counts the number of failures, and records the most recent error if any.
sections.eli5: A schedule points to a control knob on the device and says "turn this to this value at this time". The device does it automatically.

sections.title: Calendar Schedule Flexibility
sections.content:
Calendar schedules use bit fields to allow complex specifications. Setting multiple bits in a field means OR—for example, setting Monday and Friday in the weekday field triggers the schedule on both days. Setting bits across different field types means AND—setting June and July with Monday and Friday triggers only on Mondays and Fridays in June and July.

For days of the month, the RFC provides two notations. Forward notation (d1 through d31) counts from the start of the month, so d31 is the 31st day. Reverse notation (r1 through r31) counts from the end, so r1 is the last day and r31 is the first day (useful for months with fewer days).

Setting all bits in a field, or leaving it empty, means "every" for that field. For example, leaving the hour field empty means the schedule triggers at every hour.
sections.eli5: You can mix and match days, times, and months to create detailed schedules. Leaving something blank means "all of those".

sections.title: Handling Time Changes
sections.content:
When a system's clock is adjusted (for example, during daylight saving time transitions), the scheduler must handle ambiguous and non-existent times correctly. If the clock is set backward, some times appear twice; if set forward, some times are skipped.

When an action is scheduled for an ambiguous time (one that appears twice due to a backward clock adjustment), the RFC specifies that the action runs only once, at the first occurrence. When an action is scheduled for a non-existent time (skipped due to a forward clock adjustment), the RFC recommends running the action immediately when the transition occurs, in the order they would normally have run.
sections.eli5: If the clock jumps due to daylight saving time, the scheduler handles it so actions run at the right times, not twice or never.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The scheduler performs SNMP set operations on network devices, which can change device configuration or state. The RFC requires that the scheduler enforce access control rules according to the SNMP security framework. This means that a schedule can only modify MIB variables if the owner of the schedule has permission to modify them.

Each schedule entry has an owner field that identifies who created or manages the schedule. The exact semantics depend on the security policy defined by the administrator, but this provides accountability for scheduled changes.
sections.eli5: Only people with permission to change something can set up a schedule to change it. The system keeps track of who created each schedule.

items.title: Periodic
items.text: Repeats at fixed intervals (e.g., every 600 seconds)

items.title: Calendar
items.text: Triggers on specific days, times (e.g., Monday at 3 PM)

items.title: One-shot
items.text: Calendar-like but runs once and disables itself
